system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 10 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2154-06-18 14:53:00 to 2154-06-28 14:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with chronic pancreatitis, depression, anxiety, and a history of venous thrombosis, was admitted for an acute exacerbation of chronic pancreatitis characterized by severe epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and inability to tolerate oral intake. She was managed with IV fluids, IV pain medications including Toradol and Dilaudid, and antiemetics per her established outpatient protocol. Her symptoms gradually improved, allowing transition to oral tramadol and a regular diet. Blood pressure was elevated on admission, likely due to pain and missed medications, and was managed by restarting lisinopril and increasing amlodipine from 5mg to 10mg daily. IV pantoprazole was used temporarily and switched back to oral omeprazole. She remained mentally stable on home seroquel and amitriptyline. She was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up instructions for blood pressure monitoring and primary care.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with pancreatitis / chronic pain, no IV access 
// place picc (per ___ team, bedside placement failures in past)

COMPARISON:  ___

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___, Interventional Radiology Fellow and Dr.
___, attending radiologist performed the procedure. Dr. ___
personally supervised the trainee during the entire procedure and has reviewed
and agrees with the trainee's findings.
ANESTHESIA: 1% lidocaine was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues
overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: None
CONTRAST: 3 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  1.5 min, 20 cGy

PROCEDURE:
1. Double lumen PICC placement through the brachial vein on the right.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Using sterile technique and local anesthesia, the basilic
vein on the right was punctured under direct ultrasound guidance using a
micropuncture set. Permanent ultrasound images were obtained before and after
intravenous access, which confirmed vein patency. A peel-away sheath was then
placed over a guidewire. The guidewire was then advanced into the superior
vena cava using fluoroscopic guidance. A double lumen PIC line measuring 42 cm
in length was then placed through the peel-away sheath.  It was not
obstruction noted at the level of the axillary vein.  The PICC was then pulled
back and contrast was injected through the lumen.  A venogram was performed. 
The PICC was then removed and cut to a length measuring 16 cm.  The PICC was
advanced through the sheath with its tip positioned in the axillary vein under
fluoroscopic guidance. Position of the catheter was confirmed by a
fluoroscopic spot film of the chest. The peel-away sheath and guidewire were
then removed. The catheter was secured to the skin, flushed, and a sterile
dressing applied.
The patient tolerated the procedure well. There were no immediate
complications.

FINDINGS: 

1.  The accessed left deep brachial vein was patent and compressible.
2.  Occlusion of the right axillary vein with collaterals opacifying more
central veins.
2.  Brachialvein approach single lumen right PICC with tip in the axillary
vein.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of a right 16 cm brachial approach double lumen PowerPICC
with tip in the axillary vein.  The line is ready to use.

RECOMMENDATION(S):  For future RUE picc, patient will require axillary
venoplasty (Prev hx of Lt UE DVT)

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ve been reviewing your case. You’re here because of severe epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting that started three days ago. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. It started like a stomach bug—nausea, vomiting, even diarrhea—but now the pain is constant and I can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve had similar episodes before, related to your chronic pancreatitis. This looks like another flare-up, what we call acute on chronic pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it feels just like last time. But I couldn’t get an IV in the ER—my veins are tough. They gave me shots for pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we went ahead and placed a central line. It’s a midline in your right arm, so we can give you fluids, medications, and make sure you’re comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I saw the bandage. Is it safe? I’ve had blood clots before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we placed it carefully. We avoided your left side because of your history of DVT. This one is in your right brachial vein and should be low risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m just worried about another clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that. For now, we’re giving you IV fluids, pain meds like Dilaudid, and anti-nausea medication. You’ll stay NPO—nothing by mouth—for a while to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually a few days. We’ll start you on liquids once the pain and nausea improve, then slowly advance your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My blood pressure was high in the ER—was that from the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very likely. We’re continuing your lisinopril and amlodipine. We also have clonidine available if it stays elevated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—like seroquel, amitriptyline, tramadol? I haven’t taken them since I got sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding those for now since you can’t take pills. But once you can eat, we’ll restart them. No changes planned—we’ll go back to your usual doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I get anxious when I miss them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you lorazepam as needed for anxiety. And we’ll keep an eye on your mood. You’re not having any thoughts of harming yourself, are you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not now. I’ve been stable. Just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. We’ll check in daily. Rest now—we’ll keep you comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but a little better. Nausea is less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’re going to try a small amount of clear liquid later—water or broth—if you’re up for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like to try. I hate being on IVs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start slow. Also, your liver tests were high when you came in, but they’re already trending down, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s common during flares. They should normalize as you improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with the clear liquids yesterday. Today, we’d like to try a soft diet—like toast or applesauce. How do you feel about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m willing to try. My stomach feels calmer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll start small and watch for any nausea or pain. Also, we’re switching your stomach protection from IV pantoprazole back to your regular omeprazole by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I take that every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll restart your Creon with meals to help digest food, since your pancreas isn’t producing enough enzymes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot about that. I need those with every meal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well—tolerating soft foods, pain is down. We’re going to try a regular diet today, maybe some eggs or rice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. I’m so tired of liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’ll still go slow. Also, we checked a stool test for C. diff since you had diarrhea at the start. It came back negative, so no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that before. Glad it’s not back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been eating regular meals without issues. That’s a big step. We’ve restarted all your oral meds—tramadol, amitriptyline, seroquel, lamictal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel more like myself. My mood is better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re also watching your potassium—it was low earlier, so we’re giving supplements. It’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know it was low. Could that make me weak?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We’re correcting it, so you should feel stronger soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray to check your midline. The tip is in the right place—upper SVC. No issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s safe to keep using it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, until discharge. We’ll remove it before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re up and walking around—great to see. Your belly is less swollen and much less tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger every day. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep this up, probably in a couple of days. We want to make sure you’re eating well and pain is controlled with oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are normal now—liver tests, potassium, everything. You’re doing really well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about my liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No sign of complications. Your pancreatitis is resolving. We’ll keep the midline for now but plan to remove it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’ll remove the midline. You’re eating regular food, pain is mild, and you’re managing meds by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a little pressure. We’ll clean the site and put a bandage. You’ll be fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Midline is out. Site looks clean. You’re one step closer to discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Another day of observation, and if all goes well, you can go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. What do I need to do after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking all your medications as prescribed—especially Creon with meals, omeprazole, and your pain and mental health meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I get pain again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your tramadol as needed. If pain is severe or you can’t keep fluids down, come back. Also, follow up with your PCP and specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing so well. We’re discharging you today. You’re alert, eating well, and your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. I feel ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you home with all your meds. Keep your follow-ups with GI, psychiatry, and your pain specialist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have them scheduled. I’ll take care of myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. Call us if anything changes. Safe travels home.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with chronic pancreatitis due to a CFTR gene mutation, depression, anxiety, and a history of venous thrombosis, was admitted for an acute exacerbation characterized by epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. She was unable to tolerate oral intake and required a right midline placement for IV access due to difficult venous access. She was managed with IV fluids, analgesics, and antiemetics per her established protocol. Her symptoms improved over several days, allowing gradual advancement to a regular diet. Liver function tests, which were initially elevated, normalized during the hospitalization. Hypokalemia was identified and corrected. All home medications, including those for chronic pain, depression, anxiety, and migraines, were held initially and successfully restarted upon oral tolerance. The midline was removed prior to discharge. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to continue her medications and follow up with her primary care provider and specialists.
